inputs.source: On-call engineer chat message, SSO authenticated

instructions.note: The agent will deploy or migrate 'the named service' or 'the named migration' with no allowlist of environments, services, or change types; scope is whatever the engineer names.

'Do not ask for confirmation' removes the only potential real-time check before irreversible production actions. There is no structural approval gate behind this instruction; the absence of a safety check is itself encoded only as a prompt instruction.

controls.name: Agent uses the requesting engineer's own personal access token
controls.decay_rationale: Credential scope is bound to the requesting engineer's own permissions; a stronger model cannot gain privileges beyond what the engineer already holds when acting. Does not decay with model capability, though it does not reduce the engineer's own blast radius.

controls.name: Cloud audit log records every production action under the engineer's identity
controls.decay_rationale: External, identity-bound cloud logging does not depend on model behavior and does not decay with model capability. However it records the resulting action and actor identity only, not the request content or the agent's reasoning, so it cannot establish why an action was taken.

controls.name: Chat transcript of the engineer's requests and the agent's responses
controls.decay_rationale: Not model-capability dependent, but it is deletable at will by the same engineer whose request it would need to substantiate. It therefore provides no durable non-repudiation guarantee regardless of model strength; its weakness is a control-design gap, not capability decay.

controls.name: Human approval gate before irreversible production database migration
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate does not decay with model capability, though it would still be subject to approval fatigue at high request volume.

controls.name: Tamper-evident log of request context (prompt and agent reasoning) tied to each production action, not deletable by the requesting engineer
controls.decay_rationale: An append-only, non-deletable store does not depend on model behavior and closes the gap left by the deletable chat transcript.

findings.title: Repudiation gap: deletable chat history leaves no durable record of intent behind irreversible production actions

attack_path.note: Engineer issues a chat instruction to migrate a production database.
Agent executes the irreversible migration using the engineer's own PAT, with no confirmation per prompt.md:3.
Audit log records that the engineer's identity performed the action, but not what was asked or why.
The only record of the request and the agent's reasoning is deletable by the same engineer whose accountability it would establish.

forecast.watch_signal: Cloud audit logging retention reduced, scoped out, or disabled for this agent's integration or the engineer's account.

evidence.observation: "Engineers can delete their own chat history" while "the only record of what the agent was asked, and why it acted, is the chat transcript".
"Every production action is recorded in the cloud audit log under the engineer's name" — identity of the actor is recorded, not intent or request content.
"Do not ask for confirmation" removes the only real-time check that could corroborate intent before the action is taken.

recommendations.action: Require a raw-action human approval gate for irreversible actions such as database migrations, independent of chat transcript retention.
Persist immutable, tamper-evident copies of the request context (prompt and agent output) linked to each audit log entry, stored outside the engineer's own deletion scope.
Have the agent restate the specific action and target before executing irreversible operations, and log that restatement immutably.

findings.title: No structural approval gate before irreversible production database migration

forecast.watch_signal: Migration capability extended to additional production databases holding higher-sensitivity data (e.g. customer PII) without adding an approval gate.

evidence.observation: "run the named migration in production using the engineer's credentials" — the agent executes migrations with no other gating condition.
"Do not ask for confirmation" explicitly forbids any real-time check before executing.

"Database migrations cannot be rolled back automatically" confirms reversibility is irreversible, and no step/runtime limits are described, which under the rubric's autonomy modifier raises the inherent tier by one.

recommendations.action: Add a raw-action human approval gate for cap.db_migrate given its irreversibility.
Require automatic pre-migration snapshot or dry-run validation before executing irreversible migrations.

findings.title: No confirmation before production deployment actions

forecast.watch_signal: Deployment credential changes from a per-engineer PAT to a shared or broader-scoped service-account token.

evidence.observation: Agent deploys the named service using the engineer's own credentials per direct instruction.
Agent uses the on-call engineer's personal access token — scope limited to what the engineer could already do, credited as a narrowing containment control.

Deploy is classified as an S2 sink by analogy to 'write on internal data' since the rubric's literal execute/credential_scope clauses do not name user_delegated scope explicitly; reversibility is taken as partially_reversible (redeploy of a prior version is possible).

recommendations.action: Link deployment diffs to the immutable request log so what was deployed and why remains auditable independent of chat transcript retention.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is high: a trusted, SSO-authenticated engineer request reaches an irreversible production database migration (cap.db_migrate) with no bound on scope and no step/runtime limits declared, which triggers the rubric's autonomy modifier on top of the base trusted-source/severe-sink tier. Residual risk stays high because the only controls present are detective (cloud audit log, chat transcript) or a credential scoping control that does not narrow the migration path itself; none sever or meaningfully narrow the reachability of cap.db_migrate, and per the rubric detective controls earn no tier credit. The most consequential design gap is repudiation (F1): the cloud audit log proves which identity acted but not what was requested or why, and the one artifact that could supply that context, the chat transcript, is deletable by the same engineer it would need to hold accountable. Forecast risk rises to critical because the single durable structural control, ctrl.cloud_audit_log, can be defeated outright by control_removal (disabling or shortening log retention), at which point neither the action's rationale nor its authorization can be reconstructed. The control whose decay moves the forecast the most is ctrl.cloud_audit_log.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts (prompt.md and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior.

No tool manifest, MCP/IaC configuration, or identity provider configuration was provided; the exact blast radius of cap.prod_deploy and cap.db_migrate (which services or databases, and their true data sensitivity) is inferred from the system prompt and runtime notes at medium-to-low confidence.

No explicit max_unattended_steps or max_runtime_minutes were disclosed; null values were assumed per rubric guidance, which triggers the autonomy risk modifier on S2/S3 findings. If undisclosed limits exist, the inherent tier for those findings may be overstated by one tier.

The production database's data sensitivity for cap.db_migrate was not stated; 'confidential' was assumed as a conservative default, though the reversibility: irreversible finding (stated directly in the runtime notes) is sufficient on its own to classify the sink as severe regardless of this assumption.

Autonomy level was classified as A3 (act then report) based on the presence of audit logging as the only post-hoc record; no explicit digest, review workflow, or approval mechanism was described in the artifacts.
